title: "Teaching with studysim"
---

```{r}
source("_common.R")
```

Each exercise below names the scenario and options, then what the students should
find. The tables are the answer key's *expected estimates* (the average of large
simulated studies), computed by the module itself when this page was built.
*True* is the **direct** effect the data were generated with (every other
variable fixed); where a variable also acts through others, the **total** effect
follows, and *Adjusted (DAG)* adjusts each variable only for what it does not
cause.

## Confounding: coffee and coronary heart disease

*Coronary heart disease incidence*, cohort, measure age, sex, smoking and coffee.
Coffee has no effect, but coffee drinkers smoke more: the crude hazard ratio of
coffee is above 1 and disappears once smoking is in the model.

```{r}
key_table("chd_incidence", "chd", "cohort", c("age", "sex", "smoking", "coffee"))
```

Exercise: leave smoking unmeasured and show that the adjusted coffee effect stays
biased (residual confounding).

## Confounding by indication: chemotherapy

*Breast cancer prognosis*, prognosis design. Chemotherapy truly lowers the hazard
(HR 0.75), but it is given to younger women with more nodes and higher grade; its
crude hazard ratio points the wrong way.

```{r}
key_table("breast_cancer_prognosis", "death", "prognosis", c("age", "tumour_size", "nodes", "grade", "chemo"))
```

## Odds ratios from a case-control study

*Breast cancer risk factors*, case-control with two controls per case. The data are
generated as a cohort with hazard ratios; the case-control odds ratios approach them
because the disease is rare. Menopause is determined by age (a rule of the
scenario), so much of its crude odds ratio is confounding by age. After
adjustment it falls near 1, its direct effect. What remains above 1 is mediated:
only post-menopausal women take hormone replacement therapy, which is not
measured here, so menopause carries part of its effect (the *total* column).
BMI's effect, which differs before and after menopause, is centred at the
population's mean BMI, where menopause has no effect of its own.

```{r}
key_table("breast_cancer_risk", "breast_cancer", "case_control", c("age", "menopause", "parity", "family_hist", "alcohol"),
          options = list(ratio = 2))
```

Exercise: compare with *Matched case-control* on age, analysed with conditional
logistic regression.

## Effect modification

In the same scenario BMI protects before menopause and raises risk after it. A
model without the interaction gives a single, misleading BMI effect; students
should fit `bmi × menopause`. The answer key shows the true effect per level of
menopause in its note.

## Adjusting for everything: the Table 2 fallacy

*Coronary heart disease incidence*, cohort, all variables measured. Age, sex
and education act partly through blood pressure, cholesterol, BMI, diabetes and
HDL. A model with every variable gives their **direct** effects: education
seems to do nothing, and the effect of sex shrinks. Adjusting each exposure only
for its confounders (*Adjusted (DAG)*) gives the **total** effect, the one
that answers "what if this changed?". A single mutually adjusted table (the
"Table 2" of many papers) mixes both kinds.

```{r}
key_table("chd_incidence", "chd", "cohort", load_scenario(lib, "chd_incidence")$order)
```

## Trials: absolute effects and non-collapsibility

*Indomethacin after ERCP*, randomised trial. The key gives the risk in each arm,
the risk difference and the number needed to treat. The odds ratio of the
2×2 table (the marginal one) is closer to 1 than the conditional odds ratio the
data were generated with, although randomisation leaves no confounding:
adjusting for prognostic variables moves it towards the conditional one.

```{r}
trial_table("indomethacin_ercp", "pancreatitis")
```

## Biases on purpose

The *Biases* section of the panel builds a bias into the study; the answer key's
large study carries the same bias, so it shows what the biased design
estimates next to the truth. Recall bias, controls selected by exposure and the
collider act on the variables ticked in the *Exposure* column.

| bias | design | what students should see |
|---|---|---|
| Recall bias | case-control | unexposed cases report the exposure: its odds ratio inflated |
| Controls selected by exposure | case-control | hospital controls with more exposure: its odds ratio towards 1 |
| Collider (`admitted`) | cross-sectional, cohort, case-control | adjusting for a variable caused by the outcome and the exposure distorts the exposure's effect |
| Non-adherence | randomised trial | intention to treat dilutes the effect; as treated and per protocol are confounded by prognosis |
| Informative loss to follow-up | followed designs | Kaplan-Meier underestimates the risk; hazard ratios shift |
| Immortal time | cohort, prognosis | a useless treatment started during follow-up looks protective when analysed at baseline |
| Spectrum, partial verification | diagnostic | sensitivity and AUC too high with severe cases; with only some negatives verified, sensitivity too high and specificity too low |

```{r}
key_table("lung_cancer_smoking", "lung_cancer", "case_control", c("age", "sex", "smoking"),
          options = list(exposures = "smoking", recall = 0.3))
```

Recall bias of 30% on smoking (lung cancer, case-control): every smoking odds
ratio is inflated.

## Chance and bias: replicate studies

*Compare designs* with 200 *replicate studies per design*: the spread of the
estimates is the standard error a single study only estimates; a confidence
interval should contain the true value in about 95% of the studies, and power is
the share of studies that find the effect. A biased design shows a shifted
distribution and poor coverage, however many studies are drawn.

## Categorising a continuous variable

Systolic pressure in quartiles (*Form: quartiles*) gives a dose-response pattern
but loses information: compare the precision of the per-10-mmHg estimate with the
quartile contrasts, and the effect of choosing other cut points.

```{r}
key_table("chd_incidence", "chd", "cohort", c("age", "sex", "sbp"), categorize = list(sbp = list(form = "quartiles")))
```

## Trials: parallel and crossover

*Antihypertensive drug vs placebo*: in the parallel trial the unadjusted difference
is unbiased, and adjusting for baseline pressure (ANCOVA) narrows the interval. In
the 2×2 crossover each patient is their own control: 30 patients give a precise
estimate, and the period effect must be in the model.

```{r}
key_table("antihypertensive_trial", "sbp", "rct", c("sbp0", "age"))
key_table("antihypertensive_trial", "sbp", "crossover", character())
```

*Bioequivalence*: AUC and Cmax are log-normal; analyse log values and back-transform
to a geometric mean ratio, then check whether its 90% CI lies within 0.80–1.25.

## Assignments with student keys

Give every student the same options and their own **student key** (e.g. their ID):
each gets a different dataset from the same superpopulation. The teacher reproduces
any of them by typing the key, and the answer key is the same for all.

**Export class** (Output) does it in one go: type the student keys (separated by
commas) and it saves a zip with one CSV and one codebook per student, a register
of keys and seeds, and one answer key report. Students then get only their data.

A **teacher code** keeps the key out of the students' panel: typed in *Library*
before exporting a library, it locks that library; while it is loaded, the answer
key, its report, the class export, the effect sizes on the diagram, the true
values of *Compare designs* and the effects in *Library* need the code. It is a
deterrent, not protection: the library file itself holds the parameters. The
causal diagram is shown without effect sizes by default.
